subject: chemistry
question_text: Give any four characteristic properties of transition elements.

verification.note: Chapter 2 is sourced from the Sri Chaitanya Junior Fastrack chemistry section (book pp.53-55), which prints the question, its star rank and a model answer. Only ONE source book is held for chemistry — the TSBIE Basic Learning Material in hand covers physics only — so the two-book union check is PENDING a second chemistry source. The 1+1+1+1 mark split is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it; the question itself is sourced, not invented. The book lists six properties (hard heavy metals; variable oxidation states; 'colour compounds'; complex compounds; alloys; high M.P and B.P). The question asks for any four, so the card folds high melting and boiling points into the metallic-character point and alloys in with complexes, writes 'coloured compounds' for the book's 'colour compounds', and adds the one-line reasons the book omits. AI chemistry check 2026-08-25 (audit round): the insider note treated the reasons as optional while step 3 called the reason the marked phrase, so the note now says the reason is required on every point; the first step was titled 'Hard, heavy metals' while the mark split calls that mark 'Metallic character', so the step label now matches the split. No marked line changed.

page_header: Classification of Elements – Periodic Properties · 4 marks

steps.label: Metallic character
lines: 1. Transition elements are hard and heavy
metals with high melting and boiling points,
because both the ns and the (n−1)d electrons
take part in the metallic bonding.
steps.why: More electrons in the metallic bond means a stronger bond, and a stronger bond needs more heat to break — that one reason covers hardness and the high melting and boiling points together.
common_mistakes: Writing metals with no property attached. Hard, heavy and high melting point are the marked words.
Counting hard metals and high melting points as two separate properties. They come from the same bonding.
steps.memory_tip: d electrons join the metallic bond, so everything about the metal gets stronger: harder, heavier, higher melting point.
steps.margin_note: One property with its reason per numbered line; four lines earn the four marks.

steps.label: Variable oxidation states
lines: because the ns and (n−1)d electrons have
nearly equal energies and both can be lost.
steps.why: When two sets of electrons cost nearly the same energy to remove, the atom can stop after different numbers of them — that is what variable oxidation states means.
common_mistakes: Stating the property without an example. Fe²⁺ and Fe³⁺ is the expected pair.
Writing that only the d electrons are lost. The ns electrons are lost first.
steps.memory_tip: Two electron sets at nearly the same energy → more than one stopping point → more than one oxidation state.
steps.margin_note: The reason (ns and (n−1)d close in energy) lifts this from a list item to a marked point.

steps.label: Coloured compounds
lines: their ions have incompletely filled d orbitals.
Example: Cu²⁺ salts are blue, Ni²⁺ salts are
steps.why: An incompletely filled d subshell can absorb visible light when a d electron moves between its levels; the light left over is the colour we see.
common_mistakes: Writing coloured with no reason. The incompletely filled d orbitals are the marked phrase.
Using Zn²⁺ as the example. Its d¹⁰ shell is full, so zinc salts are white, not coloured.
steps.memory_tip: Partly filled d orbitals absorb visible light; a full d shell (Zn²⁺) gives white salts.
steps.margin_note: Two named examples cost one line and make the property concrete.

steps.label: Complexes and alloys

lines.text: They form complex compounds and alloys

lines: 4. Their small, highly charged ions with
empty d orbitals accept electron pairs from
other molecules to give complex compounds,
and their similar atomic sizes let the metals
mix into alloys such as brass and steel.
steps.why: Complex formation needs an ion that can accept electron pairs, and the empty d orbitals provide the space; alloy formation needs atoms of similar size that can replace one another in the metal.
common_mistakes: Naming complexes and alloys with no reason for either.
Giving a non-transition alloy example. Brass (Cu-Zn) and steel (Fe with carbon) are the expected ones.
steps.memory_tip: Empty d orbitals take electron pairs (complexes); equal-sized atoms swap places (alloys).
steps.margin_note: The question says any four, so these four with reasons are a complete answer; high M.P and B.P is already inside property 1.

insider_note: The book's answer is a bare six-item list and the question asks for any four, so four properties fill the four marks. Each numbered point must carry its one-line reason or example with it: the reason is the marked phrase, and a property named on its own is what loses the mark.
